stem: All devices that contain embedded, specialised computers are called computing devices. Identify any TWELVE computing devices used in daily life.
answer: Examples: ATM, card-payment terminal, digital washing machine, microwave oven, digital camera, smart television, CCTV camera, car engine-control unit, traffic-light controller, digital thermostat, printer and digital weighing scale. Choose devices containing embedded processing, rather than merely naming passive components.
officialNotes: 1 mark for identifying TWO devices (TWELVE required) No mark will be awarded on writing ONE device.
overall: The overall responses of the cohort to this question showed an average level of performance. The task required them to furnish instances related to embedded and specialised computer systems. Some responses showed the standard level of proficiency in this question, with a variety of additional illustrations, while some of the candidates were not able to provide precise examples of embedded or specialised systems.
better: Better responses correctly identified embedded or specialised computer systems. Additionally, the candidates enriched their answers by providing supplementary instances of embedded or specialised computers. Most candidates mentioned credit card machines, CCTV cameras, and ATMs, which is correct.
weaker: Weaker responses mentioned objects or devices that are unrelated to specialised and embedded computer systems like graphic card, hard disk and monitor, etc. By introducing irrelevant examples, the responses deviated from the set criteria. Showing real-life examples of embedded systems could enhance the conceptual understanding of the topic.

stem:
i. Describe the process of writing data on an optical disk. (2 marks)

ii. Write ONE advantage of optical storage over magnetic storage. (1 mark)
answer:
i. A recording laser changes a recording layer at selected positions to encode bits. On write-once discs it permanently changes the dye/material; on rewritable discs it changes the phase of the recording material. Different optical properties allow the encoded data to be read by a lower-power laser. Factory-pressed ROM discs use a manufacturing process rather than an ordinary disc writer.

ii. Optical storage is not erased by external magnetic fields that can affect magnetic media.
officialNotes: 1 mark for each highlighted point (TWO Required) 1 mark for writing the advantage (ONE Required)
overall: The cohort's overall response to the question was below average, revealing a misinterpretation of the process of data inscription on a hard disk. Candidates forgot to mention the important advantages of optical storage media when compared to magnetic media, showing the weaker understanding of the concepts. However, several good responses indicated better knowledge and understanding of the subject, highlighting the topic more effectively.
better: The candidates’ responses were very good, showing a precise depiction of the data writing process on a hard disk. Additionally, the candidates correctly identified the advantage of optical storage over magnetic storage like electromagnetic interference has no impact on magnetic storage devices.
weaker: Weaker responses were not precise and lacked in showing the process of writing data on a hard disk. Furthermore, in such responses, candidates did not explain why optical storage is better than magnetic storage, they wrote very general responses such as optical disk is used to store data, revealing gaps in comprehension. Addressing these aspects with greater clarity and depth would enhance the candidates’ grasp of the topic.

stem: Write any THREE differences between CISC and RISC architectures.
answer:
| Typical CISC design | Typical RISC design |
| --- | --- |
| Larger, more complex instruction repertoire | Smaller, simpler instruction repertoire |
| Often variable-length instruction encodings | Typically regular/fixed-length instruction encodings |
| May perform arithmetic directly on memory operands | Load/store design: arithmetic primarily operates on registers |

These are conventional architectural tendencies; modern processor implementations can combine techniques.
officialNotes: 1 mark for each correct difference (Any THREE required)
overall: The overall response to this question was average. Some candidates demonstrated a strong understanding of the correct differences between CISC and RISC. However, there were candidates who gave general statements or inaccurate information in the differences rather than giving differences on the basis of properties of CISC and RISC. Candidates can go through animated videos to see the working of both computer architectures.
better: Better responses correctly identified the distinctions between CISC and RISC architectures on the basis of structure and speed with precision, showcasing a clear command of the underlying principles.
weaker: In weaker responses, the fundamental distinctions between CISC and RISC architectures were mostly inaccurately explained. Mostly candidates wrote acronyms of CISC and RISC or have written that one need more instruction while other need less instruction which showed the lack of understanding of the concept.

stem:
USB is a plug-and-play port.

i. Describe plug-and-play. (1 mark)

ii. Describe the computer response when a USB device is detected. (1 mark)

iii. Name TWO devices, other than a USB flash drive, that can connect through USB. (1 mark)
answer:
i. The system detects and configures a supported device with little or no manual resource configuration.

ii. It enumerates/identifies the attached device, loads or requests the appropriate driver and configures it for use. A compatible driver may still need installation.

iii. USB keyboard and USB printer (also accept mouse, camera or scanner).
officialNotes: (a) 1 mark for description (b) 1 mark for correct answer (c) 1 mark for any two names 1 mark will be awarded on writing only one name as well.
overall: Overall, the responses to this question were average as it uses the term “plug and play” and the devices that utilise this feature, aside from USB. However, the responses received were mixed, with varying levels of accuracy and correctness. Some candidates wrote the meaning of plug and play with its examples correctly while some described the response of a computer on detecting plug and play device incorrectly resulting in loss of marks.
better: The candidates did well. Their responses showed accurate description of “plug and play” devices showing how devices can be connected to a computer system without requiring manual configuration. Candidates also provided correct examples which demonstrated a strong grip of the concept, indicating a high level of knowledge and understanding.
weaker: The candidates’ responses showcased a weak understanding of the “plug and play” concept, which is evident from the inaccurate definition and example provided like serial port and PS2 port etc. The explanation lacks precision in reflecting the working of plug and play technology, indicating a need for deeper comprehension.

stem: Differentiate infrared and Bluetooth on bandwidth, range and number of devices.
answer:
| Characteristic | Infrared (representative IrDA link) | Bluetooth (representative classic link) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data rate (called bandwidth in the question) | Early IrDA about 115.2 kbit/s; faster versions differ | Classic basic rate about 1 Mbit/s; EDR up to 3 Mbit/s gross |
| Range | Typically about 1 m with a clear optical path | Typically about 10 m for a class-2 device; class and conditions change this |
| Devices | Normally a point-to-point link between two devices | One piconet: one central/master and up to seven active peripheral/slave devices |

The question gives no technology version or device class. These are stated examples, not universal limits; Bluetooth LE has different arrangements.
overall: The cohort’s overall response to the question related to infrared and bluetooth was good. The candidates demonstrated good performance by providing accurate and relevant details about these technologies. However, certain responses were incorrect with unrelated and inaccurate information.
better: Most of the candidates’ responses effectively described the bandwidth, number of devices that can be connected and range attributes of infrared and bluetooth technologies. This showed the candidates’ good comprehension and proficiency in this topic.
weaker: Weaker responses displayed inaccuracies concerning the bandwidth and range of infrared and Bluetooth technologies. Candidates showed misconceptions by writing incorrect information regarding range of the given technologies. They also showed incorrect information in writing the number of devices that can be connected using given technologies.

stem: Differentiate primary key and candidate key.
answer:
| Primary key | Candidate key |
| --- | --- |
| One candidate key selected as the main row identifier | Any minimal set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row |
| One designated primary key per table (possibly composite) | A table may have several candidate keys |
| Selected candidate key is enforced as unique and not null | Unselected candidate keys are alternate keys and must still uniquely identify rows |

Correction to the source commentary: uniqueness is essential for every candidate key; a non-unique field is not a candidate key.
officialNotes: 1 mark for writing correct difference. (Any THREE required)
overall: The cohort’s response to this question displayed a mixed outcome. Some candidates showed accurate explanations of primary and candidate keys, defining a primary key as a unique identifier for each database record, ensuring data integrity, while some candidates presented inappropriate or erroneous details about these concepts.
better: Candidates accurately differentiated between the primary key and candidate key. They explained that there was only one primary key in a table, whereas there could be multiple candidate keys in a table. The primary key was described as crucial for uniquely identifying records, while the candidate key was not.
weaker: Weaker responses displayed general information related to primary key and candidate key. Some candidates wrote the same points for both the terminologies showing the lack of understanding of the concept.

stem:
i. Define communication device. (1 mark)

ii. Describe hub, switch and gateway. (2 marks each)
answer:
A communication device is hardware that enables data transmission or interconnection between devices/networks.

Hub: a physical-layer multiport repeater; repeats received signals to other ports without selecting a destination using MAC addresses.

Switch: learns source MAC addresses and forwards Ethernet frames to the appropriate port; separates collision domains.

Gateway: connects systems/networks using different protocols or representations and translates between them when required. A default IP gateway routes between networks; not every gateway performs application-protocol conversion.

Source terminology note: an Ethernet hub is not generally synonymous with a Token Ring multistation access unit (MAU).
officialNotes: 1 mark for the definition of communication device. 1 mark for each highlighted point in the description of Hub (Any TWO required). 1 mark for each highlighted point in the description of Switch. (Any TWO required). 1 mark for each highlighted point in the description of Gateway. (Any TWO required).
overall: As this was an ERQ, so most of the candidates attempted this part. The candidates’ response to this question was notably above average. Majority of candidates effectively defined communication device and offered satisfactory explanations for hub, switch and gateways. However, some of the candidates showed challenges in understanding the concepts and expressing their thoughts coherently.
better: The candidates’ responses were notable for their accurate definitions of communication devices. They also provided descriptions of hubs, switches and gateways, including mentioning another name for a hub, which is the multistation access unit (MAU). They explained how gateways send data packets using various protocols and mentioned that switches are intelligent devices.
weaker: The candidates’ responses showed weaknesses as they included inappropriate and irrelevant information, indicating misconceptions about the topic. Some candidates incorrectly stated that hubs and switches are the same, while others described gateways as a medium or way to send messages.

stem:
i. Define GPS. (1 mark)

ii. Describe its components. (4 marks)

iii. Mention TWO applications. (2 marks)
answer:
GPS is a satellite-based positioning, navigation and timing system.

Space segment: orbiting satellites transmit precise time and orbital information.

Control segment: ground monitoring/control stations track satellites and maintain clock/orbit information.

User segment: receivers use satellite signals and timing measurements to calculate position and time.

Applications: vehicle navigation and land surveying.

Marking discrepancy: Paper II allocates two marks to applications; the official checking hints say one mark for two applications. The paper total is seven; retain the printed allocation and record this discrepancy rather than silently changing it.
officialNotes: 1 mark for the definition of GPS. 1 mark for naming THREE components of GPS. 1 mark will also be awarded if TWO components are named. No mark will be awarded on writing only one name. 1 mark for describing each component. (THREE required) 1 mark for writing the applications of GPS. (Any TWO required)
overall: As this was an EQR, so very few candidates attempted this part with below average responses. A small number of candidates provided accurate details related to the GPS system and its practical applications. whereas, some responses displayed incompleteness and tangential references, indicating a lack of understanding for these concepts.
better: The candidates’ responses were excellent as they provided a thorough explanation of the basic aspects of the GPS system, including its components and applications. They explained how GPS functions with base stations and satellites, as well as how it provides information. Additionally, they discussed its use in navigation systems and the military.
weaker: The candidates’ responses were inadequate, featuring inaccuracies and demonstrating a limited comprehension of the relevant concepts. Some candidates mentioned the use of GPS in its definition, components, and application, resulting in marks only for the examples.

stem:
The company database contains these tables:

| Employees | Departments | Children of employees |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EmpID (primary key) | Dept_No (primary key) | Parent_Name (printed primary key) |
| Salary | Dept_Name | Age |
| Ph_No | Budget |  |

Many employees work in each department; each department is managed by an employee. Each child is identified by the employee’s name, and only one parent may work for the company. Draw an ERD.
answer:
Entities: Employees (EmpID, Salary, Ph_No), Departments (Dept_No, Dept_Name, Budget), Children_of_Employees (Parent_Name, Age). Underline the three printed primary keys when reproducing the source schema.

Relationships:

- Department — employs — Employee: one department to many employees, assuming each employee belongs to one department.
- Employee — manages — Department: each department has one manager; an employee may manage a department or none. A maximum of one managed department per employee is an explicit modelling assumption, not established by the wording.
- Employee — has dependent — Child: one employee may have many children; each child is associated with one employed parent.

Schema defect: Parent_Name alone cannot uniquely identify multiple children of one parent; employee names are also not guaranteed unique. A sound implementation adds Child_ID, or uses a composite (EmpID, Child_Name/another child identifier), and uses EmpID as the parent foreign key. Preserve the printed schema for source comparison, but do not claim that its child primary key supports the stated one-to-many relationship.
officialNotes: 1 mark for drawing all THREE entities. 1 mark for drawing attributes of all EIGHT entities. 1 mark for correctly underlining the all THREE primary keys. 1 mark for correctly writing all THREE relationship text. 1 mark for correctly writing each relationship type (THREE Required)
overall: As this was an ERQ, so few candidates attempted this part. The responses to this question were below average exhibiting limitations in the understanding of key concepts of database. Some candidates made inaccurate entity relationship diagram (ERD), which highlighted an area of deficiency in understanding and application of database concepts. Notably, no candidate accurately made the ERD, indicating a collective need for improved comprehension.
better: The candidates’ responses revealed a better understanding of table relationships in the database. It showed important connections and associations between tables, showcasing a better grasp of database design principles.
weaker: The candidates’ responses reflected a very limited grip of the topics, indicating weaknesses in understanding entity relationship diagrams (ERD) and their application. Most candidates did not mention the entities correctly or failed to establish the relationship. Those who attempted to create a relationship did not do it so correctly.

stem:
Consider the Professors table.

| Prof_ID | First_Name | Last_Name | Age | Experience_in_Years | Specialisation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| P101 | Dilawar | Khan | 47 | 22 | Accounting |
| P102 | Sana | Ahmed | 52 | 30 | Marketing |
| P103 | Faisal | Arbab | 45 | 23 | Finance |

Write MS Access SQL to:

i. Create the table, with Prof_ID as primary key; text lengths: Prof_ID 5, First_Name 20, Last_Name 15, Specialisation 25. (3 marks)

ii. Insert the last record. (1 mark)

iii. Remove Age. (1 mark)

iv. Add Gender of length 6. (1 mark)

v. Change Specialisation to length 30. (1 mark)
answer:
i.
```sql
CREATE TABLE Professors (
  Prof_ID TEXT(5) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,
  First_Name TEXT(20),
  Last_Name TEXT(15),
  Age INTEGER,
  Experience_in_Years INTEGER,
  Specialisation TEXT(25)
);
```

ii.
```sql
INSERT INTO Professors
  (Prof_ID, First_Name, Last_Name, Age, Experience_in_Years, Specialisation)
VALUES ('P103', 'Faisal', 'Arbab', 45, 23, 'Finance');
```

iii.
```sql
ALTER TABLE Professors DROP COLUMN Age;
```

iv.
```sql
ALTER TABLE Professors ADD COLUMN Gender TEXT(6);
```

v.
```sql
ALTER TABLE Professors ALTER COLUMN Specialisation TEXT(30);
```

Correction: the official e-marking INSERT example uses age 42 and experience 13, but the printed question specifies 45 and 23. The worked answer follows the question. The CREATE statement here also keeps every field inside its parentheses.
officialNotes: (i) 1 mark → CREATE TABLE Professors 1 mark → Prof_ID CHAR(5) NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, 1 mark → First_Name CHAR(20), Last_Name CHAR(15), Specialisation CHAR(25)); Age INTEGER, Experience_in_Years INTEGER, (ii) 1 mark → INSERT INTO Professors Values ('P103', 'Faisal', 'Arbab', 42, 13, 'Finance'); (iii) 1 mark → ALTER TABLE Professors DROP COLUMN Age; (iv) 1 mark → ALTER TABLE Professors ADD COLUMN Gender CHAR(6); (v) 1 mark → ALTER TABLE Professors ALTER COLUMN Specialisation Char(30);
overall: As this was an ERQ, mostly candidates attempted this part. The overall response falls within an average spectrum. Some candidates understood data types well and made the right queries, while others made mistakes in their commands, which caused them to get fewer points. It is clear that quite a few candidates might not have studied the application- level aspects of databases enough.
better: The candidates’ answers demonstrated that they understood how to make SQL queries using the right data types. They included data definition language (DDL) statements in their queries, which showed that they knew SQL programming accurately.
weaker: The candidates’ responses indicated a limited grip of constructing SQL query commands, suggesting a lack of proficiency and understanding in this area. Candidates wrote incomplete commands to create the database table based on the given criteria.
